slides.title: Every Multi-User OS Needs an Answer
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Traces to Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson's Unix (1969), specifically the Sixth Edition Unix filesystem of 1975. View inode metadata with `stat filename`.

Misconception: Students think permissions are an app-layer add-on. They are enforced by the kernel at the filesystem layer, beneath every application.

Analogy: An inode is a library card catalog entry, it tells you who owns the book and where to find it on the shelf, but is not the book itself.

Exam tip: Be ready to state that Linux permission checks happen in the kernel during every file access, not in the application.
bullets: The core question: which subjects may perform which operations on which objects?
Linux answers at the filesystem layer: permission enforcement is baked into the filesystem itself, not bolted on
The inode: every file/directory is represented by an inode storing owner, group, permission bits, timestamps, and data-block pointers
Why it matters for app security: nearly every privilege escalation, exfiltration, or persistence technique depends on a permission misconfiguration somewhere

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Traces to Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson's Unix (1969), specifically the Sixth Edition Unix filesystem of 1975. View inode metadata with `stat filename`.

Misconception: Students think permissions are an app-layer add-on. They are enforced by the kernel at the filesystem layer, beneath every application.

Analogy: An inode is a library card catalog entry, it tells you who owns the book and where to find it on the shelf, but is not the book itself.

Exam tip: Be ready to state that Linux permission checks happen in the kernel during every file access, not in the application.
content_blocks: Every multi-user operating system must answer a deceptively simple question: which subjects are allowed to perform which operations on which objects? On Linux systems, that question is answered primarily at the filesystem layer through a permission model that has remained structurally unchanged since the earliest versions of Unix.

Every file and directory is represented internally by an inode, a data structure storing all metadata about a file except its name and content: owner, group, permission bits, size, timestamps, and pointers to the disk blocks holding the data. Among those fields is a compact 16-bit permission field governing read, write, and execute access.

This model is foundational to application security because nearly every privilege escalation, data exfiltration, or persistence technique on a Linux host ultimately depends on a permission misconfiguration somewhere in the filesystem.

slides.title: Three Classes, Three Bits: The rwx Model
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: UID 0 is always root regardless of account name. `/etc/passwd` maps UIDs to usernames; `/etc/group` defines group membership.

Misconception: Students think deleting a file requires write permission on the file itself. It actually requires write permission on the parent directory.

Analogy: Three doors (owner/group/other), each with its own lock combination of read/write/execute.

Exam tip: Directory write permission governs deletion of files inside it, this directory-level rule is a frequent exam trap, tied later to the sticky bit.
bullets: Owner (user): the account associated with the file, stored as a numeric UID in the inode
Group: a named collection of accounts, stored as a numeric GID
Other (world): everyone who is neither the owner nor a group member, the most dangerous class to overprovision
Three bits per class: read (r), write (w), execute (x), nine bits total describe a file's full permission state
Displayed as a string: e.g. rwxr-xr-- from ls -l

slides.title: Three Classes, Three Bits: The rwx Model
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: UID 0 is always root regardless of account name. `/etc/passwd` maps UIDs to usernames; `/etc/group` defines group membership.

Misconception: Students think deleting a file requires write permission on the file itself. It actually requires write permission on the parent directory.

Analogy: Three doors (owner/group/other), each with its own lock combination of read/write/execute.

Exam tip: Directory write permission governs deletion of files inside it, this directory-level rule is a frequent exam trap, tied later to the sticky bit.
content_blocks: The Linux permission model divides every file's potential accessors into exactly three classes: the owner, the group, and other ("everybody else"). For each class the system tracks three independent bits: read, write, and execute.

For a regular file, read allows opening/viewing contents, write allows modifying or truncating, and execute allows running it as a program. For a directory, read allows listing contained names, write allows creating/deleting/renaming entries within it, and execute ("search"/"traverse") allows cd-ing into it or accessing known filenames inside even without read.
Because there are three classes and three bits per class, the entire permission state fits in nine bits, traditionally displayed as a string such as rwxr-xr--.

slides.title: Reading the Permission String Correctly
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Directly from the ebook's Professor's Note on reading permission strings.

Misconception: Counting the type character as part of owner's bits, producing an off-by-one misread of every subsequent triad.

Analogy: Like reading a phone number, drop the country code first, then read the remaining digits in fixed-size groups.

Exam tip: Practice decoding several `ls -l` strings until it is automatic; the exam will present raw strings and expect fast, correct triad splitting.
bullets: Four chunks: leading type character, then three triads of owner/group/other
Type character: - regular file, d directory, l symbolic link
Common mistake: miscounting the type character as part of the owner's permissions
Worked example: -rwxr-xr-- = owner rwx, group r-x, other r--
Always subtract one character first, then count triads of three

slides.title: Reading the Permission String Correctly
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Directly from the ebook's Professor's Note on reading permission strings.

Misconception: Counting the type character as part of owner's bits, producing an off-by-one misread of every subsequent triad.

Analogy: Like reading a phone number, drop the country code first, then read the remaining digits in fixed-size groups.

Exam tip: Practice decoding several `ls -l` strings until it is automatic; the exam will present raw strings and expect fast, correct triad splitting.
content_blocks: When you run ls -l and see something like -rwxr-xr--, break it into four chunks: the leading character is the file type (- for regular file, d for directory, l for symbolic link), then three groups of three characters each, owner, group, other.

So rwxr-xr-- means the owner can read/write/execute, the group can read/execute, and everyone else can only read. Students almost always miscount the leading type character as part of the owner's permissions, it is not.
This decoding skill is a prerequisite for every later topic in this chapter: octal arithmetic, special bits, and ACL auditing all start from being able to read this string correctly and quickly.

slides.title: Why This Is Coarse: The Case for ACLs
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Standardized as POSIX.1e (IEEE 1003.1e, withdrawn 1997 but implemented broadly by Linux, Solaris, BSD).

Misconception: Students think an ACL replaces the base permission bits. It supplements them; both are checked.

Analogy: The base rwx model is a building's three master keys; an ACL is a set of individually cut keys handed to specific extra people, layered on top of the master-key system, not instead of it.

Exam tip: If a scenario needs a permission the base model cannot express, name ACLs, and remember the base bits still apply underneath.
bullets: Limitation 1: cannot grant write to exactly two named users while excluding the rest of the group
Limitation 2: cannot express default permissions that automatically apply to new files created by different users
The gap-filler: POSIX ACLs layer finer-grained rules on top without replacing the base model
Critical detail: ACLs are additive, base rwx bits are always present and always evaluated, even on a file that also carries an ACL
Preview: ACL mechanics (getfacl/setfacl) covered in depth in Section II

slides.title: Why This Is Coarse: The Case for ACLs
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Standardized as POSIX.1e (IEEE 1003.1e, withdrawn 1997 but implemented broadly by Linux, Solaris, BSD).

Misconception: Students think an ACL replaces the base permission bits. It supplements them; both are checked.

Analogy: The base rwx model is a building's three master keys; an ACL is a set of individually cut keys handed to specific extra people, layered on top of the master-key system, not instead of it.

Exam tip: If a scenario needs a permission the base model cannot express, name ACLs, and remember the base bits still apply underneath.
content_blocks: The tripartite rwx model is intentionally coarse. It cannot express "grant write access to exactly these two users but not the rest of the group," nor can it express default permissions that automatically apply to new files created inside a directory by different users.

These limitations motivated the later development of POSIX ACLs, which layer finer-grained rules on top of the base model without replacing it. It is important to internalize that ACLs are additive, the base rwx bits are always present and always evaluated as part of the access decision, even on a file that also carries an ACL.

slides.title: Least Privilege: The Academic Anchor
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Saltzer & Schroeder (1975), "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems," Proceedings of the IEEE. NIST SP 800-53 control AC-6.

Misconception: Students treat least privilege as an abstract policy statement. On Linux it is a concrete, enforceable filesystem configuration decision.

Analogy: Giving a hotel housekeeper a master key to every room instead of just the rooms assigned that day, any lost key now compromises the whole hotel.

Exam tip: Connect least privilege directly to filesystem permission decisions and process identity, not just abstract policy language.
bullets: Principle of least privilege: every subject gets only the minimum permissions necessary, nothing more
On Linux, implemented via: filesystem permissions plus the identity of the account running a process
Real consequence: running a production web server as root, or leaving a config dir world-writable, enlarges the entire host's attack surface
Formalized academically: Saltzer & Schroeder (1975); codified in NIST SP 800-53 AC-6
Inheritance rule: a compromised process inherits exactly the permissions of the account that runs it

slides.title: Least Privilege: The Academic Anchor
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Saltzer & Schroeder (1975), "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems," Proceedings of the IEEE. NIST SP 800-53 control AC-6.

Misconception: Students treat least privilege as an abstract policy statement. On Linux it is a concrete, enforceable filesystem configuration decision.

Analogy: Giving a hotel housekeeper a master key to every room instead of just the rooms assigned that day, any lost key now compromises the whole hotel.

Exam tip: Connect least privilege directly to filesystem permission decisions and process identity, not just abstract policy language.
content_blocks: The principle of least privilege, one of the oldest and most rigorously validated concepts in computer security engineering, is, on a Linux host, implemented almost entirely through filesystem permissions and the identity of the user account under which a process executes.

When a system administrator runs a production web server as the root superuser instead of a dedicated unprivileged service account, or leaves a configuration directory world-writable for developer convenience, they are not making a stylistic choice; they are directly enlarging the attack surface of the entire host, because any process that is compromised, a vulnerable PHP script, a malicious npm package, a misconfigured cron job, inherits exactly the permissions of the account that runs it.

slides.title: Still Relevant in the Cloud-Native Era
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Directly from the ebook's Real-World Context callout, connecting this topic forward to container case studies in Section III.

Misconception: 'Containers are isolated, so filesystem permissions inside don't matter.' Namespace-shared UID 0 can defeat that isolation, as Section III's case study shows.

Analogy: A shipping container still obeys the physics of the truck carrying it, the container abstraction rides on top of the same underlying rules.

Shared UID space: a container 'root' user is frequently the same UID 0 as the host's root unless namespace remapping is configured
Cloud storage too: AWS EFS and Google Filestore still enforce rwx bits underneath their web consoles
Takeaway: raw Linux permission knowledge is the substrate modern cloud-native security tooling is built on
Not legacy knowledge: still directly tested by real-world container misconfiguration incidents (Section III)

slides.title: Two Notations, One Command: chmod
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: POSIX.1-2017 §chmod; on Linux implemented in GNU coreutils; underlying syscall is chmod(2)/fchmodat(2).

Misconception: Students think any user with write access can chmod a file. Only the owner (or root) can, regardless of write permission.

Analogy: Only the person who owns a locker (or the building superintendent) can change its lock combination, a guest with borrowed access cannot.

Exam tip: Know both notations cold; the exam tests conversion in both directions.
bullets: chmod: "change mode", the utility that modifies a file's permission bits, POSIX.1-2017 standard
Only owner or root may invoke chmod on a given file
Octal notation: numeric weights summed per class (read=4, write=2, execute=1)
Symbolic notation: targeted deltas using u/g/o/a class specifiers with +/-/= operators
Both accepted by chmod, every security-conscious admin must be fluent in both

slides.title: Two Notations, One Command: chmod
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: POSIX.1-2017 §chmod; on Linux implemented in GNU coreutils; underlying syscall is chmod(2)/fchmodat(2).

Misconception: Students think any user with write access can chmod a file. Only the owner (or root) can, regardless of write permission.

content_blocks: The nine permission bits are most commonly manipulated using two complementary notations: octal notation and symbolic notation. Both notations are accepted by the chmod ("change mode") command, and every security-conscious systems administrator must be fluent in both.
Only the file's owner or a superuser may invoke chmod on a given file, an unprivileged non-owner cannot change a file's mode even if they could otherwise access it.

slides.title: Octal Arithmetic: r=4, w=2, x=1

quiz.question: A file must allow the owner full control, the group to read the file but not modify or run it, and must not be exposed to any other account. What is the correct chmod value?
quiz.explanation: 640 is correct: owner=rw- (4+2=6), group=r-- (4), other=--- (0). Note the owner does NOT need execute here since the scenario only specifies full control over data, not execution; the ebook's worked exam trap uses exactly this pattern. 750 wrongly gives group execute, 664 wrongly gives other read access, 600 wrongly denies the group entirely.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Memorize the weights cold: read=4, write=2, execute=1, every combination 0-7 is a unique sum.

Misconception: Students add weights incorrectly when a bit is absent, a missing bit contributes 0, not a placeholder value.

Analogy: Like binary place values (1,2,4) read out as a single digit per class, each bit is independently on or off.

Exam tip: A classic exam trap: 'owner needs full control, group needs read-only, other needs nothing' → chmod 640. Practice converting rapidly in both directions.
bullets: Weights: read=4, write=2, execute=1, summed per class
Worked example: rwxr-xr-x = owner 4+2+1=7, group 4+0+1=5, other 4+0+1=5 → 755
Every combination 0-7 is unique: 0=none, 1=x, 2=w, 3=wx, 4=r, 5=rx, 6=rw, 7=rwx
Common patterns: 755 for executables, 644 for config files, 600 for private keys
Verification: always confirm with ls -l after a chmod

content_blocks: Octal notation assigns numeric weights to each permission: read is worth 4, write is worth 2, execute is worth 1. Summing the applicable weights for each of the three classes (owner, group, other) produces a three-digit number that fully describes the file's mode.

A permission of rwxr-xr-x, for example, is computed as owner = 4+2+1 = 7, group = 4+0+1 = 5, other = 4+0+1 = 5, yielding chmod 755, a typical mode for an executable script or binary. 644 is typical for a plain configuration file (owner read+write, everyone else read-only), and 600 is typical for a private SSH key (owner read+write, nobody else anything).

code_block.content:
# Grant the owner full control, group and other read+execute only
# Typical mode for an executable script or binary
chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh

# Grant the owner read+write, group and other read-only
# Typical mode for a plain configuration or data file
chmod 644 /etc/myapp/app.conf

# Grant the owner full control, deny group and other entirely
# Typical mode for a private SSH key or credential file
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

# Verify the resulting mode
ls -l /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh
# -rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 812 Jul  9 09:14 /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh

slides.title: Symbolic Notation: Targeted Deltas
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Defined in POSIX.1-2017 for the chmod utility.

Misconception: Students use lowercase x in a recursive chmod and accidentally make every data file executable. Capital X avoids this.

Analogy: Symbolic mode is like editing a document with tracked changes (add/remove specific edits) versus octal's 'retype the whole paragraph' approach.

Exam tip: Recognize g+rX,o+rX recursive patterns as the safe way to open read access on a web tree without breaking scripts or exposing data files as executable.
bullets: Class specifiers: u (user/owner), g (group), o (other), a (all)
Operators: + (add), - (remove), = (set exactly)
Use case: automated deployment scripts wanting an idempotent change without knowing the prior mode
Capital X: applies execute only to directories/files that already have execute for someone, safe for recursive operations
Full removal: chmod o= path strips all 'other' permissions

slides.title: Symbolic Notation: Targeted Deltas
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Defined in POSIX.1-2017 for the chmod utility.

Misconception: Students use lowercase x in a recursive chmod and accidentally make every data file executable. Capital X avoids this.

Analogy: Symbolic mode is like editing a document with tracked changes (add/remove specific edits) versus octal's 'retype the whole paragraph' approach.

Exam tip: Recognize g+rX,o+rX recursive patterns as the safe way to open read access on a web tree without breaking scripts or exposing data files as executable.
content_blocks: Symbolic notation, by contrast, applies targeted deltas rather than restating the full mode. The syntax combines a class specifier (u, g, o, or a for all), an operator (+ to add, - to remove, = to set exactly), and one or more permission letters. Symbolic mode is especially useful in automated deployment scripts where you want to guarantee an idempotent state change without needing to know or preserve the file's prior mode.

A useful detail: capital X applies execute only to directories and files that already have execute for someone, it will not make plain data files unexpectedly executable during a recursive operation, unlike lowercase x.

slides.title: Symbolic Notation: Targeted Deltas
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Defined in POSIX.1-2017 for the chmod utility.

Misconception: Students use lowercase x in a recursive chmod and accidentally make every data file executable. Capital X avoids this.

Analogy: Symbolic mode is like editing a document with tracked changes (add/remove specific edits) versus octal's 'retype the whole paragraph' approach.

Exam tip: Recognize g+rX,o+rX recursive patterns as the safe way to open read access on a web tree without breaking scripts or exposing data files as executable.

code_block.content:
# Add execute permission for the owner only, leaving group/other untouched
chmod u+x install.sh

# Remove write permission from the group, and set other to read-only exactly
chmod g-w,o=r /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

# Recursively grant read+execute to group and other on a directory tree
chmod -R g+rX,o+rX /var/www/html
# Note: capital X applies execute only to directories and files that
# already have execute for someone -- it will not make plain data files
# unexpectedly executable during a recursive operation.

# Remove all permissions from other on a sensitive directory
chmod o= /etc/myapp/secrets

slides.title: chown and chgrp: Ownership Is a Separate Axis
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: POSIX.1-2017 §chown/§chgrp; underlying syscall for chown is chown(2).

Misconception: Students assume chgrp requires root like chown does. It does not, as long as the user is a member of the target group and owns the file.

Analogy: chown is like transferring a car's title (only a notarized authority can do it); chgrp is like adding a household member as an authorized driver (you can do that yourself).

Exam tip: Know that ownership (chown/chgrp) and permission bits (chmod) are independent, orthogonal controls that are typically applied together during deployment.
bullets: chown: reassigns the user (and optionally group) that owns a file, root-only on standard configurations
chgrp: reassigns only the group; an ordinary user CAN chgrp a file they own to any group they belong to
Why root-only for chown: prevents ordinary users from giving away files to dodge disk quota accounting
Frequently paired with chmod during deployment to hand runtime files to a service account
Syntax: chown newuser:newgroup filename

slides.title: chown and chgrp: Ownership Is a Separate Axis
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: POSIX.1-2017 §chown/§chgrp; underlying syscall for chown is chown(2).

Misconception: Students assume chgrp requires root like chown does. It does not, as long as the user is a member of the target group and owns the file.

Analogy: chown is like transferring a car's title (only a notarized authority can do it); chgrp is like adding a household member as an authorized driver (you can do that yourself).

Exam tip: Know that ownership (chown/chgrp) and permission bits (chmod) are independent, orthogonal controls that are typically applied together during deployment.
content_blocks: Ownership itself is a separate axis from permission bits, and is modified with chown and chgrp. These utilities are frequently paired with chmod during application deployment to ensure that a service account, rather than the deploying administrator's personal account, ends up as the effective owner of runtime files.

Only the superuser can transfer ownership of a file to a different user on standard Linux configurations, because allowing ordinary users to give away files could be abused to circumvent disk quota accounting. Unlike full ownership transfer, an ordinary user may chgrp a file they own to any group they themselves belong to, without needing root privileges.

code_block.content:
# Transfer ownership of the web root to the unprivileged www-data service account
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html

# Change only the group of a shared log directory to "loggers"
sudo chgrp -R loggers /var/log/myapp

# Combine ownership transfer with a permission reset in one deployment step
sudo chown deploy:deploy /opt/myapp/release && sudo chmod 750 /opt/myapp/release

slides.title: Special Bits: setuid, setgid, Sticky
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Octal values: setuid=4000, setgid=2000, sticky=1000. Displayed respectively as 's' (owner x position), 's' (group x position), 't' (other x position).

Misconception: Students think write permission on a directory alone lets any user delete files inside freely. Without the sticky bit that IS true, which is exactly why /tmp needs it despite being world-writable.

Analogy: setuid is a borrowed VIP badge that always grants the badge-owner's access level no matter who is wearing it; the sticky bit is a rule that only the person who dropped an item in a shared bin may remove it.

Exam tip: Know all three special bits' octal values and displayed symbol positions, this is a frequent direct-recall question.
bullets: Fourth octal digit: written to the left of the standard three, e.g. chmod 4755
setuid (4000): executable runs with the owner's effective privileges regardless of who launches it, displayed as 's' replacing owner's x
setgid (2000) on executable: same idea but for the group
setgid on directory: new files/subdirs inherit the parent directory's group automatically, standard technique for shared collaborative directories
Sticky bit (1000): on a directory, restricts deletion/renaming to the file owner, directory owner, or root, displayed as 't'

Misconception: Students think write permission on a directory alone lets any user delete files inside freely. Without the sticky bit that IS true, which is exactly why /tmp needs it despite being world-writable.

Analogy: setuid is a borrowed VIP badge that always grants the badge-owner's access level no matter who is wearing it; the sticky bit is a rule that only the person who dropped an item in a shared bin may remove it.

content_blocks: Beyond the base nine bits, Linux defines three special permission bits occupying a fourth octal digit conventionally written to the left of the standard three. setuid, when set on an executable file, causes the program to run with the effective privileges of the file's owner rather than the privileges of the user who launched it, regardless of who launches it. The classic example is /usr/bin/passwd.

setgid on an executable functions like setuid but for the group. On a directory, setgid has an entirely different and extremely useful effect: any new file or subdirectory created inside it automatically inherits the parent directory's group, rather than the creating user's primary group, the standard technique for maintaining consistent group ownership on shared collaborative directories.

The sticky bit, when set on a directory, restricts deletion and renaming of files within that directory so that only the file's owner (or the directory's owner, or root) may remove or rename it, even if other users have write permission on the directory itself.

sudo chmod 2775 /srv/shared/project

slides.title: Critical Concept: setuid Root Binaries Are Privilege Escalation Gold

quiz.question: Why is a setuid binary owned by root considered a high-value privilege escalation target?
options: It always contains a known software bug
It runs with root's effective privileges no matter which unprivileged user invokes it, so an exploitable flaw in it grants root access
It bypasses network firewalls
It disables ASLR for the invoking process
quiz.explanation: Option B is correct: setuid causes execution with the file owner's (root's) effective privileges regardless of invoker, so if the binary can be manipulated (symlink race, argument injection, shell escape), an unprivileged user gains root. Option A is false, many setuid binaries are safe by design. Options C and D describe unrelated mechanisms.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: GTFOBins (gtfobins.github.io) is a real, actively maintained catalog of exploitable behaviors in common Unix binaries, many involving setuid.

Misconception: Students think setuid itself is a bug. It is a deliberate, necessary feature (e.g. passwd), the danger is an EXPLOITABLE setuid root binary, not the mechanism's mere existence.

Analogy: A master key left in a lock that anyone can turn if they find the right trick, the key's existence is intentional, but an unguarded exploitable trick turns it into a full building compromise.

Exam tip: Be ready to explain WHY a setuid root binary is dangerous (privilege inheritance regardless of invoker) and name the mitigation (minimize + audit).

Exploitation paths: symlink race, unsanitized argument, or shell escape from within the program
Result: attacker escalates from an ordinary account straight to root
Real tooling: GTFOBins catalogs 'living off the land' privilege escalation through legitimately installed setuid binaries
Baseline control, not optional: auditing find / -perm -4000 output on every hardened host

slides.title: POSIX ACLs: Closing the Granularity Gap
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Part of the acl package (libacl) on Linux, implementing the withdrawn POSIX.1e draft standard.

Misconception: Students think ACLs replace rwx checking. Both are evaluated; ACLs add named-user/group entries on top of the base classes.

Analogy: ACLs are like adding named exceptions to a general building policy, 'everyone in Sales may not enter the server room, except Alice, who may look but not touch.'

Exam tip: Know getfacl reads, setfacl writes, a simple but frequently tested pairing.
bullets: The gap: base rwx cannot express 'grant read-only to exactly one additional user, alice, on an otherwise restricted file'
getfacl: displays the full ACL, base entries plus named-user/group entries plus the effective rights mask
setfacl: adds, modifies, or removes ACL entries; can set a default ACL for automatic inheritance on new files
Requires: filesystem mounted with the acl option (default on most modern ext4/XFS mounts)
Storage: ACL entries live as extended attributes on the inode, alongside but separate from the base rwx bits

content_blocks: The base rwx model, even augmented with special bits, still cannot express arbitrarily granular permission grants, for example, "grant read-only access to exactly one additional user, alice, on a file otherwise restricted to the owner." This is the precise gap that POSIX ACLs close.

ACLs are inspected using getfacl and modified using setfacl. A default ACL can also be set on a directory so that new files created within it automatically inherit specific ACL entries, the ACL analogue of the setgid bit's inheritance behavior, but far more flexible.

code_block.content:
# View the current ACL on a file
getfacl /srv/shared/report.csv
# file: srv/shared/report.csv
# owner: bob
# group: finance
# user::rw-
# group::r--
# other::---

# Grant read-only access to a single additional user, alice,
# without changing the base owner/group/other bits

# Grant read+write to a specific group, auditors, on a directory,
# and set a default ACL so new files inherit the same entry

setfacl -d -m g:auditors:rwx /srv/shared/reports

# Remove a specific ACL entry
setfacl -x u:alice /srv/shared/report.csv

# Strip all extended ACL entries and revert to the base rwx bits only

slides.title: Evaluation Order and the Telltale Plus Sign
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This evaluation order and the '+' indicator are exactly what a security auditor checks first when reviewing sensitive files.

Misconception: Assuming a file with mode 600 (owner-only) is airtight without checking for a trailing '+' that could indicate a broader ACL grant.

Analogy: A locked front door (base mode) that looks secure, but there's also a side door with a spare key given to someone else (the ACL), you have to check both to know the real access picture.

Exam tip: If a scenario shows a permission string ending in '+', immediately flag that getfacl must be run to see the full access picture before drawing conclusions.
bullets: Kernel evaluation order: owner rwx first, then named-user ACL entries, then group + named-group ACL entries (subject to the mask), then other
The tell: a trailing + after the permission string in ls -l output signals an ACL is present
Auditor trap: a seemingly restrictive base mode can conceal a permissive ACL grant layered on top
Practical rule: never trust a base mode alone on a file showing the +, always run getfacl to see the full picture
Effective rights mask: caps the maximum permission any ACL entry can actually grant, even if the entry itself requests more

content_blocks: A recurring class of real-world Linux privilege escalation findings, documented repeatedly in penetration testing reports and in automated privilege-escalation enumeration tools such as LinPEAS and linux-exploit-suggester, involves scripts referenced by cron jobs that are misconfigured with overly permissive filesystem permissions.

In a representative incident pattern, a system administrator creates a maintenance script and places it in a directory referenced by a root-owned crontab entry. During initial setup, to avoid troubleshooting permission errors, the administrator runs chmod 777 on the script or its containing directory "temporarily," intending to tighten it later. That tightening step is frequently forgotten.

slides.title: The Escalation Mechanics: How the Attack Actually Runs
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This is a textbook example of the Section I principle in action: a broken filesystem permission directly enlarges the attack surface of the whole host.

Misconception: Confusing this with a setuid escalation. The privilege here comes from WHO invokes the script (root's cron daemon), not from a setuid bit on the script itself.

Analogy: Slipping a forged instruction into a manager's daily to-do list, the manager (root/cron) will faithfully carry out whatever is written there next time they check it.

Exam tip: Be able to trace the causal chain: world-writable script → attacker edits it → cron (running as root) executes edited content → root-level payload runs.
bullets: Inheritance, not setuid: the script executes with root's privileges because cron invokes it, not because of any setuid bit
The write: any local user who can write to the world-writable script can append/replace its contents with arbitrary commands
Payloads: adding the attacker's account to sudoers, or spawning a setuid root shell
Timing: the next cron firing (often within minutes) executes the injected payload with full root privileges
Rated severity: one of the most commonly identified 'quick win' privilege escalation paths in professional pentest engagements

slides.title: Case Study: Containers Running as Root
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Docker released 2013; OCI standardized image/runtime formats 2015-2017. Bind mounts: `docker run -v /host/path:/container/path`.

Misconception: 'Containers are isolated, so what happens inside stays inside.' Isolation is enforced by namespaces/cgroups sharing the host kernel, a shared UID space plus a bind mount defeats that isolation for filesystem access.

Analogy: A see-through vault door labeled 'isolated' that happens to use the exact same master key as the building's front door, the label promises separation the mechanism doesn't actually provide.

Exam tip: Connect this directly back to Section I's 'still relevant in the cloud era' concept, this case study is that concept's concrete failure mode.
bullets: The old problem, new instance: containerization reintroduces the root-privilege problem in a new form
Default UID 0: Docker containers run as UID 0 by default unless explicitly configured otherwise
Shared UID namespace: container UID 0 is the SAME numeric ID as the host's actual root, absent dedicated remapping
Bind mounts: mounting a host directory into a container makes it the literal same inode, not a copy
The exposure: a compromised container process with a bind mount is root with respect to that host path's permission checks

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Docker released 2013; OCI standardized image/runtime formats 2015-2017. Bind mounts: `docker run -v /host/path:/container/path`.

Misconception: 'Containers are isolated, so what happens inside stays inside.' Isolation is enforced by namespaces/cgroups sharing the host kernel, a shared UID space plus a bind mount defeats that isolation for filesystem access.

Exam tip: Connect this directly back to Section I's 'still relevant in the cloud era' concept, this case study is that concept's concrete failure mode.
content_blocks: The rise of containerization introduced a new instance of an old permission problem. By default, unless explicitly configured otherwise, processes inside a Docker container run as UID 0, the same numeric root UID used by the host operating system's actual superuser account, because Linux user IDs are a single global namespace shared between the host and any container that does not use dedicated UID remapping.

If an operator mounts a host directory into a container as a bind mount and that container's main process is compromised, for instance, through a vulnerable web application dependency, the attacker's shell inside the container is running as root with respect to that bind-mounted host directory's permission checks, even though the container is nominally "isolated."

slides.title: Not a Linux Flaw, A Design Decision Failure

quiz.question: A security team discovers that a Docker container running a web application was compromised, and the attacker was able to overwrite the host's SSH authorized_keys file. Explain how this was possible given that the container was assumed to be 'isolated,' and identify whether this represents a flaw in the Linux permission model itself.
quiz.prompt: Address: (a) the role of shared UID 0 namespace; (b) the role of the bind mount; (c) whether this is a Linux permission flaw or a configuration failure, and why.
quiz.explanation: Full-credit response: (a) Docker containers run as UID 0 by default, which is the same numeric root UID as the host unless user namespace remapping is configured, so the container process is root with respect to any filesystem the kernel lets root touch. (b) A bind mount makes a host directory directly accessible inside the container as the same underlying inode, not a copy, so writes from inside the container are immediately real writes to the host filesystem. (c) This is NOT a flaw in the Linux permission model, the kernel correctly enforced that UID 0 can write to the mounted path, exactly as rwx/ownership rules specify. The actual failure was the configuration decision to run the container as root with an unnecessarily broad, writable bind mount; the fix is running as a non-root UID (Dockerfile USER directive or --user flag) and using read-only (:ro) mounts wherever write access is not genuinely required.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Modern container tooling supports explicit unprivileged UID (USER directive, --user flag) and read-only bind mounts specifically to reintroduce least privilege at the container layer.

Misconception: Blaming 'Linux permissions' for the incident. The kernel did exactly what the (misconfigured) UID and mount told it to do, the fault is in configuration choice, not the enforcement mechanism.

Analogy: A perfectly functioning alarm system that was simply never armed, the hardware isn't broken, someone chose not to use it correctly.

Exam tip: If asked 'is this a Linux permission flaw or a configuration failure,' the correct framing is almost always configuration/design failure, with permissions enforced correctly underneath.
bullets: Documented pattern: multiple CVEs against container runtimes/orchestration tooling show variations of this pattern
Attack targets: SSH authorized_keys files, systemd unit files, or parts of the host root filesystem via overly broad mounts
The key insight: this is NOT a flaw in Linux permissions, they are enforced exactly as designed
Real failure: the decision to run the containerized process as UID 0 with unnecessary write access to host paths
Modern remediation: USER directive in Dockerfile, or --user at runtime, and read-only (:ro) bind mounts

quiz.question: A security team discovers that a Docker container running a web application was compromised, and the attacker was able to overwrite the host's SSH authorized_keys file. Explain how this was possible given that the container was assumed to be 'isolated,' and identify whether this represents a flaw in the Linux permission model itself.
quiz.prompt: Address: (a) the role of shared UID 0 namespace; (b) the role of the bind mount; (c) whether this is a Linux permission flaw or a configuration failure, and why.
quiz.explanation: Full-credit response: (a) Docker containers run as UID 0 by default, which is the same numeric root UID as the host unless user namespace remapping is configured, so the container process is root with respect to any filesystem the kernel lets root touch. (b) A bind mount makes a host directory directly accessible inside the container as the same underlying inode, not a copy, so writes from inside the container are immediately real writes to the host filesystem. (c) This is NOT a flaw in the Linux permission model, the kernel correctly enforced that UID 0 can write to the mounted path, exactly as rwx/ownership rules specify. The actual failure was the configuration decision to run the container as root with an unnecessarily broad, writable bind mount; the fix is running as a non-root UID (Dockerfile USER directive or --user flag) and using read-only (:ro) mounts wherever write access is not genuinely required.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Modern container tooling supports explicit unprivileged UID (USER directive, --user flag) and read-only bind mounts specifically to reintroduce least privilege at the container layer.

Misconception: Blaming 'Linux permissions' for the incident. The kernel did exactly what the (misconfigured) UID and mount told it to do, the fault is in configuration choice, not the enforcement mechanism.

Analogy: A perfectly functioning alarm system that was simply never armed, the hardware isn't broken, someone chose not to use it correctly.

Exam tip: If asked 'is this a Linux permission flaw or a configuration failure,' the correct framing is almost always configuration/design failure, with permissions enforced correctly underneath.
content_blocks: Multiple publicly documented incidents and vulnerability disclosures (including numerous CVEs against container runtimes and orchestration tooling) have demonstrated variations of this pattern: an attacker who achieves code execution inside a root-privileged container with an insufficiently scoped bind mount can write directly to sensitive host paths, achieving full host compromise from what was assumed to be a sandboxed application environment.

This is not a flaw in Linux permissions themselves; it is a demonstration that the rwx and ownership model is being correctly enforced exactly as designed, and that the actual security failure was the decision to run the containerized process as UID 0 with unnecessary write access to host paths in the first place. A container boundary is not a substitute for correct Linux permission hygiene, it is an additional layer that still depends on correct permission hygiene underneath it.

code_block.content:
# Create a dedicated, non-interactive service account for an application
sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin svc_myapp

# Web root: readable and executable by the service account, not writable
sudo chown -R root:svc_myapp /var/www/myapp
sudo find /var/www/myapp -type d -exec chmod 750 {} \;
sudo find /var/www/myapp -type f -exec chmod 640 {} \;

# Uploads directory: the one path the service account IS allowed to write to,
# scoped narrowly and with the sticky bit to prevent cross-user file tampering
sudo mkdir -p /var/www/myapp/uploads
sudo chown svc_myapp:svc_myapp /var/www/myapp/uploads
sudo chmod 1770 /var/www/myapp/uploads

# Confirm the service process itself runs as the unprivileged account, not root
ps -eo user,pid,cmd | grep myapp-server

slides.title: Layer 2: Routine Filesystem Auditing

quiz.question: During a routine audit, a security engineer finds a directory with mode 777 that does NOT have the sticky bit set, and multiple unrelated users have files inside it. What is the specific risk this configuration creates?
options: The directory cannot be read by any user
Any user with access to the directory can delete or rename files belonging to other users, since directory write permission alone governs deletion
The directory's files will automatically inherit setuid permissions
Files in the directory cannot be executed by anyone
quiz.explanation: Option B is correct: without the sticky bit, deletion/renaming within a writable directory is governed solely by write permission on the DIRECTORY, not ownership of the individual file, so any user with directory write access can delete or rename other users' files. This is exactly why /tmp requires both world-writable AND sticky (mode 1777). Options A, C, and D describe unrelated or fabricated effects.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This directly operationalizes the Section III lesson that 'temporary' chmod 777 changes are reliably forgotten, the audit is the systematic catch mechanism.

Misconception: Treating a one-time audit as sufficient. The whole premise is that drift is CONTINUOUS, so auditing must be recurring/automated, not a single pass.

Analogy: A building fire-code inspection isn't done once at construction, it recurs annually because things drift out of compliance over time.

Exam tip: Memorize the four audit categories conceptually: world-writable files, world-writable+no-sticky directories, setuid/setgid binaries, orphaned ownership.
bullets: Why: permission misconfigurations accumulate silently, debugging shortcuts, incomplete scripts, forgotten temp grants
Audit 1: world-writable files outside expected scratch/temp locations
Audit 2: world-writable directories missing the sticky bit, a red flag on any shared directory
Audit 3: every setuid/setgid binary system-wide for manual review
Audit 4: files with no valid owner (orphaned UID), often left behind after account deletion

code_block.content:
# Find world-writable files outside of expected scratch/temp locations
find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 -not -path "/tmp/*" -not -path "/var/tmp/*"

# Find world-writable directories missing the sticky bit (deletion is NOT
# restricted to file owners -- a red flag on any shared directory)
find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000

# Find every setuid/setgid binary system-wide for manual review
find / -xdev \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -type f 2>/dev/null

# Find files with no valid owner (orphaned UID, often left behind
# after an account was deleted without reassigning its files)
find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup 2>/dev/null

slides.title: Layer 3: ACLs and CIS Benchmarks for Granular Cases
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Published and updated by the Center for Internet Security (cisecurity.org); automated tools OpenSCAP and Lynis check compliance against CIS Benchmark controls directly.

Misconception: Students think 'more open' is always simpler and safer to reason about than an ACL. In practice a documented ACL exception is more auditable and precise than a broadened base permission.

Analogy: Building a specific, labeled side entrance for the delivery team (ACL) instead of just leaving the main door unlocked for everyone (broadened base permission).

bullets: Deliberate ACL use: when the base model can't cleanly express a needed pattern, use ACLs deliberately and document them
Anti-pattern: broadening base 'other' permissions as a workaround instead of using a properly scoped ACL
CIS Benchmarks: consensus-developed, vendor-neutral hardening guides from the Center for Internet Security
Concrete example: /etc/shadow must never be readable by any account other than root
Contrast example: /etc/passwd stays world-readable but never world-writable, legacy utilities depend on reading it

slides.title: Exam Focus: Layered Filesystem Defense

quiz.question: Using the five-layer filesystem defense model, diagnose which layer(s) failed in the Section III cron privilege-escalation case study, and specify the exact remediation for each failed layer.
quiz.prompt: Address: which of the 5 layers (identity, base permissions, special bits, ACL, audit) failed, and what specific command or practice fixes each.
quiz.explanation: Full-credit response: Layer 2 (base permissions) failed directly, the script/directory was left at chmod 777 instead of a least-privilege mode; remediation is chmod 700 or 750 restricted to the admin account that needs to edit it. Layer 5 (continuous audit) also failed, a routine `find / -perm -0002` sweep would have caught the world-writable file before exploitation; remediation is scheduling this audit to run automatically (e.g., via its own properly-permissioned cron job). Layer 1 (identity) is not directly implicated since the script correctly needed to run as root for its maintenance function, but Layer 1 reasoning still applies in spirit: only the specific script needed root, not a whole broadly-writable directory. Layers 3 and 4 (special bits, ACL) were not the primary failure here, though a sticky bit on the containing directory could have added defense in depth.

Misconception: Naming only one control (e.g. 'they should use chmod') when the exam wants the full layered reasoning across identity, base, special bits, ACL, and audit.

Analogy: A bank vault has a guard (identity), a locked door (base permissions), a time-lock (special bits), a visitor exception list (ACL), and security camera review (audit), all five, not just one.

Exam tip: When asked to diagnose the cron or container case studies from Section III, map the failure explicitly onto one or more of these five layers.

Layer 3, Special bits: setgid for shared collaborative inheritance, sticky for shared writable dirs, setuid audited and minimized
Layer 4, Granular control: POSIX ACLs for exceptions the base model cannot express
Layer 5, Continuous audit: automated scans (CIS Benchmark tooling, find -perm sweeps) to catch drift over time

Misconception: Students think audit tooling uses some exotic technique. It is the same octal-digit arithmetic from Section II, just automated and run at scale.

Analogy: The demo is a flight simulator for the audit sweep, safe to run, but the underlying decision logic is identical to a real find command.

Exam tip: Be able to explain, in plain language, what each octal digit position and value means when reading a simulated or real audit finding.

code_block.content:
# Toy model of a permission audit sweep (runs in Pyodide)
files = [
    {"path": "/tmp", "mode": "1777"},                 # world-writable + sticky: OK
    {"path": "/srv/scratch2", "mode": "0777"},         # world-writable, NO sticky: FLAG
    {"path": "/usr/bin/passwd", "mode": "4755"},       # setuid root: FLAG for review
    {"path": "/etc/myapp/app.conf", "mode": "0644"},   # normal config file: OK
    {"path": "/srv/shared/project", "mode": "2775"},   # setgid shared dir: FLAG for review (expected)
]

def audit(files):
    findings = []
    for f in files:
        mode = f["mode"].zfill(4)
        special, owner, group, other = mode[0], mode[1], mode[2], mode[3]
        world_writable = int(other) in (2, 3, 6, 7)
        has_sticky = special in ("1", "3", "5", "7")
        has_setuid = special in ("4", "5", "6", "7")
        has_setgid = special in ("2", "3", "6", "7")
        if world_writable and not has_sticky:
            findings.append(f"FLAG world-writable no-sticky: {f['path']} ({f['mode']})")
        if has_setuid or has_setgid:
            findings.append(f"REVIEW special bit present: {f['path']} ({f['mode']})")
    return findings

for line in audit(files):
    print(line)

slides.title: Synthesis: The Permission Misconfiguration Kill Chain
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This kill-chain framing mirrors the classic cyber kill chain concept taught elsewhere in the AP Cybersecurity curriculum, specialized here to filesystem permission misconfigurations.

Misconception: Treating each case study (cron, container, setuid) as structurally different. All three instantiate the identical five-step pattern with different specific mechanisms at steps 1 and 4.

Analogy: Three different burglaries (a window left unlocked, a spare key under the mat, a borrowed master key) that all follow the identical five-act structure: opportunity created, opportunity persists unnoticed, opportunity discovered, opportunity leveraged, and the actual theft/escalation.

Exam tip: When given ANY Linux permission incident scenario, map it onto these five steps explicitly, this is a strong, transferable free-response structure.
bullets: Step 1, Introduction: an overly broad permission is granted, often 'temporarily' during setup or debugging
Step 2, Persistence of the gap: the broad grant is never reverted; no audit catches it
Step 3, Discovery: an attacker (or pentest tool like LinPEAS) enumerates the filesystem and finds the misconfiguration
Step 4, Leverage: the attacker writes to the over-permissioned path (a cron script, a bind-mounted host directory, a setuid binary)
Step 5, Escalation/Impact: a privileged process (root's cron, a root container process) executes the attacker's change, or a setuid binary hands over root

content_blocks: Every incident pattern examined in this topic, the cron case study and the container case study, follows the same five-step kill chain, and recognizing this shared structure is more valuable than memorizing each incident as a separate story.

Step 1: an overly broad permission is introduced, typically as a shortcut during setup, debugging, or default configuration (chmod 777, default UID 0 in a container). Step 2: that gap persists because no routine audit catches it, this is the human/process failure Section IV's auditing layer exists to close. Step 3: an attacker, whether a human pentester or automated tooling like LinPEAS, discovers the misconfiguration through enumeration. Step 4: the attacker leverages the writable path, editing a cron script, writing through a bind mount, or invoking an exploitable setuid binary. Step 5: a privileged execution context (root's cron daemon, a root-UID container process, or the setuid binary's owner privilege) carries out the attacker's payload, completing the escalation.

slides.title: Interrupting the Kill Chain: Where Each Layer Breaks It
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This slide operationalizes defense in depth: no single layer needs to be perfect if multiple layers each independently reduce the chance the full kill chain completes.

Misconception: Believing a single strong control (e.g. 'we audit weekly') is sufficient on its own. Layered defense assumes any one control can fail or be incomplete.

Analogy: A series of nets under a tightrope walker, no single net needs to be perfect if there are several, because a fall through one still gets caught by the next.

Exam tip: Given a described breach, identify which kill-chain step succeeded that a specific hardening control should have interrupted, this is a very likely FRQ pattern.
bullets: Breaks Step 1: proper least-privilege configuration from the start (750/640 patterns, dedicated service accounts, USER directive)
Breaks Step 2: routine automated auditing (find -perm sweeps, CIS Benchmark scans) catches the drift before an attacker finds it
Breaks Step 3: reduces attack surface generally, but discovery is hard to fully prevent, assume adversaries will enumerate
Breaks Step 4: ACLs and narrowly scoped writable paths (sticky-bit-protected uploads dirs) limit what leverage is even possible
Breaks Step 5: FIM/detection tooling (AIDE, Tripwire) and setuid minimization reduce the odds a privileged context ever executes the payload

content_blocks: Each layer of the Section IV hardening model maps onto a specific point where the kill chain can be interrupted, reinforcing why layered defense in depth matters more than any single control. Preventing Step 1 (introduction of the broad grant) is the cheapest intervention, correct configuration from the start via service accounts and least-privilege modes.

Preventing Step 2 (persistence) is the job of routine auditing. Step 3 (discovery) is difficult to prevent outright since a determined attacker with local access will eventually enumerate the filesystem, so defenders should assume it will happen. Step 4 (leverage) is blocked by scoping writable paths as narrowly as possible, using ACLs for genuine exceptions rather than broad grants. Step 5 (escalation) is the last line of defense, FIM tooling and minimized setuid attack surface reduce the chance that a privileged context ever actually executes the attacker's payload.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: A synthesis slide to consolidate before assessment, echoing 5.1's closing structure.

Misconception: Treating this topic as a list of unrelated commands (chmod, chown, setfacl) rather than one coherent least-privilege enforcement system.

bullets: One model, nine bits: owner/group/other × read/write/execute is the foundation everything else extends
Two notations: octal (weighted sum) and symbolic (targeted delta) both configure the same underlying bits via chmod

content_blocks: Topic 5.2 rests on a single organizing idea: Linux filesystem security is the continuous discipline of keeping actual permission state matched to least-privilege intent. The nine-bit owner/group/other model, configured via chmod's octal and symbolic notations, is the foundation; special bits (setuid, setgid, sticky) and POSIX ACLs extend it to handle identity-inheritance and fine-grained edge cases the base model cannot express.

The two anchor case studies, world-writable cron scripts and root-privileged containers with bind mounts, demonstrate that the Linux kernel enforces permissions exactly as configured; real incidents trace back to human configuration decisions, not flaws in the enforcement mechanism itself. The five-layer hardening model (identity, base permissions, special bits, ACLs, continuous audit) and the five-step kill chain (introduction, persistence, discovery, leverage, escalation) together provide a complete, reusable framework for both designing secure filesystem configurations and diagnosing incidents when that discipline lapses.

big_idea.text: The principle of least privilege is a hotel key card that opens only your room and the gym — never the master key that happens to open every door on every floor, 'just in case' someone needs it.
